newsitem.title: USA: Independent BoE right step for UK and EMU-Dresdner.
newsitem.headline: Independent BoE right step for UK and EMU-Dresdner.

text.p: The British government's decision to make the Bank of England fully independent is a "right step in the right direction" for Britain to join European Monetary Union (EMU), a Dresdner Bank AG director said on Tuesday.
"This is one key element to prepare the United Kingdom for a participation in the EMU," Ernst-Moritz Lipp, a member of Dresdner's board of managing directors, told Reuters.
"It's the right step in the right direction," said Lipp, who presented a paper on the single European currency at a conference of the Bankers' Association for Foreign Trade.

But Lipp cautioned against concluding that the independence of the Bank of England, effective on Tuesday, means Britain will be part of the first wave of nations to adopt the Euro as their currency in 1999.

Granting the Bank of England its independence is one of the first decisions taken by Britain's Prime Minister Tony Blair since he took office on Sunday. Blair's Labour Party looks more favorably on joining the EMU than do the Conservatives who lost their parliamentary majority in elections last week.
"I cannot imagine they (Blair's government) have decided now to join in 1999 because the date is so close," Lipp said.

"But this is an ideal situation for Europe that the U.K. is ready to prepare itself for the monetary union. They need some time to change the mental readiness to get into the EMU," Lipp added. "With the steps announced, it would not take very long for the U.K. to join not very long after 1999. The attitude of the new government is much more constructive toward Europe."
But Lipp said the parity at which the British pound would join the Euro was a question mark due to sterling's volatility against other European currencies like the mark.
Lipp was confident Germany will meet the EMU deficit criteria and be with France in the Euro core group in 1999.
"It's difficult to predict at what conversion rate the pound would enter the Euro if the U.K. government decides to join...because of its volatility in recent years," Lipp said.
The Dresdner director cited the Benelux countries, Austria, Ireland, Portugal and Finland as other candidates for the 1999 Euro deadline.
"Switzerland certainly will not join in 1999. But after a period of time, if everything goes well, it will," he said.
Lipp also predicted the Euro would start off as a strong currency versus the dollar and the yen, propped up by a relatively tight monetary policy by the European central bank.

"The European central bank will take a tough attitude. Interest rates will be set in a tough way to increase the confidence in the new currency," said Lipp, who stressed "the biggest challenge of the central bank will be to create confidence."
Lipp saw room for foreign exchange speculations only in the "very short period" directly preceding the 1999 deadline, after which fundamentals would determine the Euro parity.
"The exchange rate between the Euro and the U.S. dollar will be determined on both sides of the Atlantic by interest rate differentials and business cycles issues," he said.
He also expected European nations to continue to exert fiscal discipline once their debt is converted to Euros which would lead corporate issuers to issue their debt in Euros as well.
